lesson.title: Checking Text Boundaries: startswith() and endswith()
lesson.summary: The startswith() and endswith() methods return True or False by checking only the beginning or end of a string against a pattern, offering a safer alternative to manual slicing.
lesson.body:
Sometimes you do not need to know where a substring is, only whether a string begins or ends with a particular piece of text. That is precisely what .startswith() and .endswith() are for: two boolean-returning string methods that check the very start or very end of a string against a pattern you supply, without scanning the whole string the way .find() does.

Calling text.startswith("Dr.") returns True if the string literally begins with the exact characters "Dr." and False otherwise. Trace "Dr. Alvarez".startswith("Dr."): Python checks the first three characters of the string, 'D', 'r', '.', against the pattern "Dr.", finds an exact match, and returns True. Compare that to "Mrs. Alvarez".startswith("Dr."), where the first three characters are 'M', 'r', 's', which do not match "Dr.", so the result is False. .endswith() works the same way but checks the tail of the string instead: "report.pdf".endswith(".pdf") returns True because the last four characters are exactly ".pdf".

These methods are case-sensitive by default, just like .replace(), so "dr. alvarez".startswith("Dr.") returns False because lowercase 'd' does not match uppercase 'D'. When you want a case-insensitive check, combine it with .lower() first: text.lower().startswith("dr."), converting the whole string to lowercase before comparing against a lowercase pattern. This is the same normalize-then-compare strategy introduced with Upper and Lower Methods, applied here to a different kind of check.

A genuinely useful real pattern is filtering a list of filenames by extension:

files = ["notes.txt", "photo.png", "report.pdf", "essay.txt"]
text_files = [f for f in files if f.endswith(".txt")]
print(text_files)  # ["notes.txt", "essay.txt"]

This list comprehension walks through every filename in files and keeps only the ones whose last four characters match ".txt", producing exactly two matches from the original four. Both .startswith() and .endswith() also accept a tuple of possible patterns instead of a single string, so f.endswith((".txt", ".md")) returns True if the filename ends with either extension, which is handy when you need to match more than one pattern without writing multiple or conditions.

Why use these instead of .find() or slicing? Clarity and correctness both. Writing text[:3] == "Dr." works, but it silently behaves oddly if text is shorter than three characters, since slicing beyond the end of a string does not raise an error in Python, it just returns whatever characters exist. .startswith() handles that edge case cleanly and reads as exactly what it means, which makes your intent obvious to anyone reading the code later, including yourself.

These methods also show up constantly when validating URLs and file formats. Checking url.startswith(("http://", "https://")) before trying to open a web address is a standard safety check, confirming the string at least looks like a web address before your program spends time trying to use it. Anywhere you catch yourself reasoning about "what does this text begin or end with," reach for these two methods before reaching for .find() or manual slicing.
